Selling a house in Indianapolis

Indianapolis is the Indiana capital and the seat of Marion County, a consolidated city-county whose limits match the county except for four separate towns and cities: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and Speedway. Nine civil townships divide the county: Center, Decatur, Franklin, Lawrence, Perry, Pike, Warren, Washington and Wayne. A house in Perry Township or Pike Township is in a real map location with its own schools, fire and assessor boundaries.

The 2020 count was 887,642 residents. The median owner-occupied home value is $224,800, and 56.0% of households own their homes, which means nearly half rent. That matters if your house has tenants. These are citywide medians, and a home in a historic district and a house on a street with several vacant lots can sit far from them, so treat the numbers as context and not as a price for your property.

Large employers such as Eli Lilly, Amazon and FedEx shape housing demand, and an owner facing a transfer or relocation may want a sale on a set date.

Older houses and historic districts

Indianapolis was a planned city, laid out in 1821 as a one-mile-square grid around a central circle. Housing followed the transit lines, and the streetcar suburbs include Broad Ripple, Irvington and University Heights. The city has 13 local historic districts and five conservation areas, among them Chatham-Arch, Fountain Square, Lockerbie Square, Old Northside, Irvington and Woodruff Place.

Age shows up in the details a buyer prices in:

  • Original knob-and-tube wiring or older panels in pre-war homes.
  • Clay or cast iron sewer laterals under mature trees.
  • Brick foundations, wet basements and old plaster.
  • Exterior changes in a historic district that may need review before work starts.

The city counts roughly 500 registered neighborhood associations, so an association may also have rules about exterior work or signs.

Weather and flood zones

Indianapolis has hot summers, cold winters and rain in every month, with 42.4 inches of rain and 25.9 inches of snow in a typical year. The record high is 106 degrees and the record low is minus 27. That swing is hard on roofs, gutters, driveways and HVAC equipment.

The White River runs 31 miles through the city and is fed by about 35 streams, including Eagle Creek, Fall Creek, Pleasant Run and Pogue's Run. Homes near those waterways may sit in mapped flood zones, and a lender may require flood insurance. Check the parcel on FEMA's flood map service before you list.

  • Check the gutters and grading if a basement has ever taken water.
  • Keep receipts for roof or drainage work, since buyers ask.
  • Photograph any storm damage before repairs.

Rentals, short-term rentals and vacant houses

Owners of residential rental units must register them, and the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services (DBNS) runs the registry. If you are selling a rented house, the lease, the registry record and any open code issues all become part of the sale conversation.

Short-term rentals have their own permit program, in effect since January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no fee for renewals. The unit must be a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code.

Vacant houses face the Continuous Vacancy program, which began January 1, 2026 and targets homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can last up to two years, and negligent owners can be fined up to $5,000 per year, with fines adjusted if the owner works with DBNS. If you inherited a vacant Indianapolis house, call DBNS before the problem grows.

Before the Marion County Recorder will record a deed, the Assessor's Office has to stamp it. Have your title company, attorney or another preparer draw up the deed itself. Filing can be done by mail, through e-recording partners or in person. Your title company can estimate how long recording will take after closing.

Indiana transfers also carry a sales disclosure form under IC 6-1.1-5.5-3. Buyer and seller complete it, the county assessor reviews it, and the county auditor files it ahead of the conveyance document.

  • Confirm any open code orders with DBNS.

Taxes and the homestead deduction

Indianapolis owners pay property tax in two installments, May 10 and November 10. Whichever falls close to your sale date gets prorated by the closing agent, and tax still owed comes out of your proceeds at closing. Call the county treasurer if you want today's balance before you accept an offer.

Owners who live in the house may benefit from the state homestead deduction, which is the lesser of $45,000 or 60% of gross assessed value. Ask the county auditor how it applies to your bill.

Steps from first call to closing

  2. We look at the property and make an offer.
  3. If you accept, the title company searches the deed for liens, unpaid taxes and open code orders.
  4. You sign the deed and the sales disclosure form.
  5. The Assessor's Office stamps the deed, the Recorder records it, and you are paid.

Delays usually come from the title search. A payoff letter, a stale registry record or a code order nobody has closed can each add days. Mention them early.

What Indianapolis sellers usually face

Sellers who want speed usually fit one of a few patterns, and the pattern sets the pace of the sale.

  • An inherited house that needs probate, clean-out or repairs.
  • A rental with a tenant, postponed maintenance or a registry question.
  • A vacant house that has drawn code attention.

  • A job move that leaves a mortgage and an empty house behind.

Cash can sidestep lender appraisals and repair demands, though a normal listing deserves a side-by-side comparison.

Get the offer in writing, find out who pays for title and recording, and read the contract before signing. On the first call, have your tax bill, payoff figures and any lease close at hand.

If the house is inherited

An inherited house in Indianapolis may need probate before a deed can be prepared, and it may also need a clean-out. Heirs often live elsewhere and carry the utilities, insurance and tax bill while the house sits. If the property is empty, check with DBNS about vacancy rules before the problem grows. Collect the estate papers, the tax bill and the keys before you talk to a buyer or the title company, and ask what the deed needs.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to register a rental house in Indianapolis before selling?

Owners of residential rental units in Indianapolis are required to register them with the city. If the house is currently rented, make sure the registry record is current so the sale paperwork lines up.

How long does recording a deed take in Marion County?

The deed must first be stamped by the Assessor's Office in Room W121, then submitted by mail, e-recording or in person. Your title company can tell you the timing for your closing.

Does Indianapolis have a short-term rental permit?

Yes. A permit program began January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no renewal fee. The unit must be a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code.

What is the Continuous Vacancy program?

It is a DBNS program that began January 1, 2026 for vacant homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can run up to two years, and fines can reach $5,000 per year.

Can I sell an Indianapolis house that needs major repairs?

Allen County's seat lies in northeastern Indiana, 18 miles from the Ohio line. The St. Joseph, the St. Marys and the Maumee rivers all come together here. Flood history and flood zones

Water is the defining weather event here. In the Great Flood of 1913, seven people died, about 15,000 lost their homes and more than 5,500 buildings were damaged. A second flood in 1982 sent 9,000 residents out and damaged 2,000 buildings, at a cost of $56.1 million in 1982 dollars. A $50 million flood control project followed, Headwaters Park among its pieces.

A normal year brings about 38 to 39 inches of precipitation and about 33.5 inches of snow. Look up your property's flood zone and any insurance requirement before you list. A buyer's lender will check regardless, and an unexpected answer can push a closing back.

School districts and getting around

Public schools come from four districts: Fort Wayne Community Schools (the largest in Indiana), East Allen County Schools, Northwest Allen County Schools and Southwest Allen County Schools. Your mailing address is not a reliable guide to which one covers you, so use the district's boundary tool before you describe schools to a buyer.

I-69 is the lone Interstate through town, with I-469 looping around it as the beltway. U.S. Routes 24, 27, 30 and 33 and State Roads 1, 3, 14, 37 and 930 fill in the rest. Commercial flights use Fort Wayne International Airport, and Smith Field serves general aviation. About 85 percent of residents drive to work alone.

In Allen County, distribution, transportation and logistics hold 23.1 percent of jobs and health care 17.9 percent.

A job transfer or layoff is a common reason a family needs to sell quickly. If the house also needs repairs, a slow listing gets expensive.

Code enforcement and vacant properties

Minimum housing standards are enforced by Neighborhood Code Compliance, an office within Community Development. Its work includes unsafe structures, securing vacant buildings and cleaning up blight, along with tall grass and weeds, abandoned or inoperable vehicles, and a protocol for properties tied to meth.

  • Phone: 311 or 260-427-1127.
  • Office: 200 E. Berry St., Suite 320, Fort Wayne, IN 46802.

Chapter 152 of the city code lets inspectors enter with probable cause or the owner's consent. If entry is refused, they can ask for a warrant under Indiana Code 36-7-9-16. A vacant building that is unsealed and unsecured can be declared a public nuisance and receives a full inspection.

Since 2015 the statewide Blight Elimination Program has paid for 259 demolitions in the city, with money from the U.S. Treasury passed through the Indiana Housing and Community Development Authority. Does your house have an open order to repair or demolish? Say so at the start. It affects the price and the route to closing, but a sale is still possible.

Visit the Allen County Treasurer at the Rousseau Centre, 1 E. Main St., Suite 104, or write to PO Box 2540, Fort Wayne, IN 46801. The phone is 260-449-7693. On closing day you sign the deed, and the title company handles the recording and the payoffs. Because the unpaid-tax figure and any open city order are settled ahead of time, the day itself is mostly signatures. If you live out of town, ask the title company whether you can sign by mail. Those details are worth asking about in the first conversation rather than the last. Plan on a few days between accepting the offer and the signing, since the title search comes first.

Without a lender, no appraisal can send the buyer back to the table for a lower price. The trade is a price below a fully renovated retail sale, so compare what you would net from a listing after repairs, commission and carrying costs.

Evansville housing market

Evansville is the Vanderburgh County seat, on a bend of the Ohio River in southwestern Indiana. It is the third-largest city in the state, with 117,298 people at the 2020 census and an estimate of 116,176 as of July 2025. The city covers about 47.9 square miles.

Owners hold a slim majority of housing at 54.6%. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $143,100, owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,150 a month, and median gross rent is $975. The city has 53,095 households averaging 2.12 people.

Thirteen neighborhoods are listed as National Register historic districts, and Riverside is known for tree-lined brick streets and turn-of-the-century homes. Indiana's seller disclosure form asks whether a property sits in a locally designated historic district, so owners in those areas should have an answer ready.

Flood risk and the levee system

Evansville sits behind a levee system built after the 1937 Ohio River flood. The river crested at 53.7 feet on January 31, 1937, the flood covered about 500 city blocks, and the city was placed under martial law.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began construction in 1939 and finished in 1994. The system includes 17 miles of earth levees and concrete floodwalls plus 19 pumping stations, and it protects against flood water up to 57 feet. The Evansville-Vanderburgh Levee Authority District maintains it.

  • The eastern levees closely follow I-69.
  • Pigeon Creek has been widened and leveed, and Ohio River backwater affects the whole county.
  • The creek's average annual peak flow at the Fort Branch gauge rose from about 2,350 to 2,820 cubic feet per second over 35 years.

Indiana's seller disclosure asks whether you know the property is in a FEMA flood plain. A buyer or lender may also want flood zone and insurance details, so find out your parcel's status before you sell. Humid summers and about 45 inches of rain a year make roof condition, drainage and basement moisture standard inspection topics too.

Older homes and the local economy

Downtown grew from an original plat of about 200 acres and still holds early twentieth-century buildings. Hardwood furniture made Evansville a manufacturing center, with 41 factories by 1900, and many of the older houses around town date from that era. Homes of that age often have original roofs, wiring and plumbing that buyers want priced in.

Today health care, manufacturing and finance employ many residents. Deaconess Health System and Ascension St. Vincent are major health care names, Berry Global and OneMain Financial are headquartered here, and two universities, the University of Evansville and the University of Southern Indiana, bring students and staff. Job changes at employers like these are one reason homes come up for sale on short notice.

Indiana property tax is due in two installments, in May and November. A payment up to 30 days late carries a 5% penalty, and one later than that carries 10%. Payments go to the Vanderburgh County Treasurer. When you sell, the closing agent normally settles the tax with you and the buyer, so ask for a figure before the settlement date.

The Building Commission, in Room 310, can tell you whether an inspection or permit is open on the house.

Most sellers have some balance to clear. Ask your lender for a payoff letter and the Treasurer for the current tax figure. Both come out of your proceeds at closing, and you receive the rest. With a cash sale you decide how fast this happens, and no buyer's lender has to approve the house before the money is released.

If the house is a rental, bring the registration paperwork and any code notices. If an estate owns it, bring the court paperwork and the names of every heir. If the house sits near Pigeon Creek or the river, tell us what you know about past water. Honest answers up front keep the closing on schedule.

Do Evansville landlords have to register their rental properties?
